This unit's own bytes open without a header, a woe cry, a divine-speech frame, or a judgment announcement, closing instead on an asylum plea and a Davidic-throne promise; the retained massa_oracle value is disclosed here as an operative-category deviation from the judgment content the label ordinarily carries, held for its place within the header-bounded Moab burden.

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: This chapter is a single sign-act report bounded by its own narrative onset, “In the year that Tartan came to Ashdod” (web:Isa.20.1), and the command frame "בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא דִּבֶּ֣ר יְהוָה֮ בְּיַ֣ד יְשַׁעְיָ֣הוּ" (oshb:Isa.20.2, byte tier) -- a time-frame and messenger clause continuing, in the same verse, into an imperative to strip off sackcloth and sandals and the compliance clause reporting it done, “He did so, walking naked and barefoot.” (web:Isa.20.2). The interpretation opens with its own divine-speech onset, "וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֔ה" (oshb:Isa.20.3, byte tier), “Yahweh said,” (web:Isa.20.3); the servant reference naming the sign-actor is explicit rather than one of the unnamed servant-figure zones elsewhere in the book: "עַבְדִּ֥י יְשַׁעְיָ֖הוּ" (oshb:Isa.20.3, byte tier), "my servant Isaiah," names the prophet himself, “As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and a wonder concerning Egypt and concerning Ethiopia,” (web:Isa.20.3). Although narrated in the third person from start to finish rather than as a first-person report, the whole chapter is held as one row bounded by the sign-act's own narrative frame: the divine-speech onset at Isa.20.3 does not open a fresh narrative episode but supplies that same episode's own explanation of the sign already performed and completed in Isa.20.2, and no new narrative-onset marker -- a fresh time-frame or scene turn -- recurs to divide it.
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading this unit as narrative_prose parallel to the later court narrative is a defensible alternative label to vision_report, since the whole account is third-person past-tense narration of a sign-act rather than a first-person vision report; the operative-category deviation is disclosed here rather than argued away.
